entry: Extrajudicial killing by a group. It is usually an informal public execution by a mob to punish an alleged transgressor or intimidate others. In the United States, where the word probably arose during the [[American Revolution]], the practice became linked to frontier vigilante justice and to mob attacks on [[African Americans]], which were frequent in the South after the [[Reconstruction era]]. Black people are thought to have been the primary victims, about 72% of the total. In Europe, lynching was common during the [[French Revolution]] and the 1848 Revolutions, targeting political opponents and nobles. It persisted in the former Russian Empire after the [[October Revolution]].

36th president of the United States (1963–69), a Texas Democrat who had been vice president under [[John F. Kennedy|Kennedy]]. He assumed office after the [[Assassination of John F. Kennedy|assassination]] of Kennedy in 1963 and won the 1964 election in a landslide, with the largest share of the popular vote for the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] in history. Johnson's Great Society programs included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, and the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]], followed by the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Public frustration with the [[Vietnam War]] and domestic unrest reduced his approval, and he withdrew from the 1968 race after a disappointing New Hampshire primary. Historians rank his domestic record in the upper tier, while his foreign policy is heavily criticized.

Genus of four extant species of medium-sized wild cats in the family [[Felidae]]. Lynxes have a short tail, black tufts on the ear tips, and large, padded paws suited to walking on snow. The smallest species are the [[Bobcat|bobcat]] and the Canada lynx, and the Eurasian lynx is the largest. They are usually solitary, and mating takes place in late winter. Each year the female gives birth to between one and four kittens after a gestation of about 70 days, and the young stay with her for about nine months. Their prey ranges from deer to snowshoe hares, foxes, squirrels, fish and birds. They live in high-elevation forests with dense cover, and the Eurasian lynx ranges from central and northern Europe across Asia.

American Southern rock band. The group was formed in [[Jacksonville, Florida]] in 1964 and popularized Southern rock with songs such as "Sweet Home Alabama" and "Free Bird". A plane crash on October 20, 1977, killed lead singer Ronnie Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines and backup singer Cassie Gaines. The band reformed in 1987 with Johnny Van Zant on vocals. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked it No. 95 on its 2004 list of the "100 Greatest Artists of All Time", and it was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2006.

City in east-central [[France]], at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers (pop., 2023: 519,127). Lyon is the third-largest city in France, and its metropolitan area is the second largest. The capital of the Gauls under the Roman Empire, it grew into a major economic hub during the [[Renaissance]] and was historically important for silk weaving. The city has played a significant role in cinema history since Auguste and Louis Lumière invented the cinematograph there. Old Lyon, the Fourvière hill, the Presqu'île and the slopes of the Croix-Rousse are inscribed on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]]. Lyon is a major center of banking, chemical, pharmaceutical and [[Biotechnology|biotech]] industries. It also hosts the international headquarters of [[Interpol]] and [[Euronews]]. The Fête des lumières, a four-day festival that begins every 8 December, has earned the city the title "Capital of Lights".

Small constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere, one of the 88 modern constellations. Its name is Latin for *lyre*, and it represents the lyre of [[Orpheus]] in Greek mythology. Its brightest star, [[Vega]], forms a corner of the Summer Triangle asterism. Beta Lyrae is the prototype of a class of [[Binary star|binary stars]]. The constellation also hosts the [[Ring Nebula]], the second-discovered and best-known planetary nebula. It is bordered by [[Draco (constellation)|Draco]], Hercules, Vulpecula and [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]].

Stringed instrument of the [[Lute|lute]] family, classed as a yoke lute. Lyres were used in several ancient cultures around the [[Mediterranean Sea]], and the earliest known examples date to c. 2700 BC in Mesopotamia. The eastern, or flat-based, lyres of the [[Fertile Crescent]] were found in Egypt, Syria, Anatolia and the Levant. The round lyre, which also originated in Syria and Anatolia, died out in the east c. 1750 BC but reappeared in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] c. 1700–1400 BC and later spread throughout the [[Roman Empire]]. The round lyre gave rise to the Germanic lyre or rotte, widely used in north-western Europe from pre-Christian to medieval times. In ancient Greece, the instrument accompanied vocal performances and lyric poetry.

Either of two species of ground-dwelling Australian birds in the genus *Menura*. Lyrebirds are named for their outer tail feathers, which are broad and curved in an S-shape that resembles a [[Lyre|lyre]]. They are large [[Passerine|passerine]] birds able to mimic a wide variety of natural and artificial sounds. During courtship the male fans its huge tail. Lyrebirds are ancient Australian animals, and the Australian Museum holds fossils about 15 million years old. Lyrebirds form the family Menuridae, which contains only this genus. The birds have unique plumes of neutral-colored tailfeathers and are among Australia's best-known native birds. Their closest relatives are generally thought to be the scrub-birds, though a link to bowerbirds remains controversial.

Ancient Greek comedy by [[Aristophanes]]. It was first staged in early 411 BC at the Lenaea festival in [[Classical Athens|classical Athens]]. Lysistrata, an Athenian woman, persuades women from warring Greek city-states, including [[Sparta]], to withhold sex from their husbands until the men negotiate an end to the [[Peloponnesian War]]. The women seize the [[Acropolis of Athens|Acropolis]], which holds the state treasury. The play satirizes male warmongering through farce and inverted gender roles, and it was produced two years after Athens's defeat in the Sicilian Expedition. Its structure departs from the conventions of Old Comedy, a shift typical of Aristophanes' career. The play has influenced later adaptations in theater and literature.

Membrane-bound organelle found in animal cells, though not in [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]], and rarely in [[Plant cell|plant cells]]. They serve as the cell's degradation center, breaking down proteins, polysaccharides and lipids into amino acids, monosaccharides and free fatty acids. Their acidic interior, isolated by a single lipid membrane, contains over 60 different hydrolases, enzymes that work best at low pH. They measure 0.1–1.2 μm and take in extracellular particles by endocytosis and intracellular components by autophagy. They also contribute to plasma membrane repair, energy metabolism, cell signaling and the immune response. Belgian scientist Christian de Duve is credited with discovering lysosomes in the 1950s and was awarded the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

American six-barreled rotary [[Machine gun|machine gun]] firing 7.62×51mm NATO rounds at 2,000 to 6,000 rounds per minute. Its external [[Electric motor|electric motor]] drives the rotating barrels, and its ancestor is the [[Gatling gun]], which was later electrically powered. The term minigun originally denoted a General Electric model. In the 1960s, the [[United States Armed Forces]] began exploring modern variants for use in the [[Vietnam War]], where helicopters proved vulnerable to small-arms fire. Several U.S. military branches use it, designated M134 and XM196 by the Army and GAU-2/A and GAU-17/A by the Air Force and Navy.

American [[Assault rifle|assault rifle]] adapted from the ArmaLite AR-15 for the U.S. military. Entering service as the M16 in 1964, it was deployed for jungle warfare in the [[Vietnam War]] the following year. The M16A1 replaced the M14 as the standard U.S. service rifle in 1969. The [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] adopted the M16A2 in 1983 and the Army followed in 1986. Total worldwide production is approximately eight million, making it the most-produced firearm of its 5.56mm caliber. In frontline units the M4 carbine has largely replaced it. In April 2022 the Army selected the SIG MCX SPEAR, designated M7, to replace the M16 and M4.

Single-action, recoil-operated semi-automatic pistol chambered primarily for the .45 ACP cartridge. Designed by John Moses Browning, it was adopted by the U.S. Army in 1911 as the standard sidearm, the first semi-automatic pistol in widespread military service. Problems with .38-caliber revolvers in the [[Philippine–American War]], where stopping power proved inadequate, helped prompt its development. It remained in service through [[World War I]], [[World War II]], the [[Korean War]] and the [[Vietnam War]]. It was formally replaced by the 9mm Beretta M9 in 1985, but its design principles continue to influence modern handguns. Special operations units still favor it for its proven performance.

American third-generation main battle tank, named for General Creighton Abrams. Designed by Chrysler Defense, it entered service in 1980 as one of the heaviest tanks in use, at nearly 73.6 short tons (66.8 metric tons). It introduced a multifuel turbine engine, Chobham composite armor and a computer fire control system to U.S. armored forces. It was developed from the failed joint MBT-70 project with [[West Germany]], and its first combat use came in the [[Gulf War]]. It later saw service in the [[Iraq War]] and the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|War in Afghanistan]], and Ukraine has used it in the [[Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)|Russo-Ukrainian war]].

[[World War II]] medium tank used widely by the United States and Western Allies. The British named it after General William Tecumseh Sherman, and it evolved from the M3 Lee with an emphasis on reliability and ease of production. The M4 was the most-produced American tank of the war, and only the Soviet [[T-34]] exceeded its output, with approximately 84,070 units built. Its 75 mm gun gave it an edge over German tanks when it first fought at the Second Battle of El Alamein in late 1942. It later served in the [[Korean War]] and with [[Israel]].

Entactogen with stimulant and minor psychedelic properties, commonly known as ecstasy or molly. First synthesized in 1912 by Merck chemist Anton Köllisch, it was used to enhance psychotherapy from the 1970s and became popular as a street drug in the 1980s. Attendees of dance parties, raves and [[Electronic dance music|electronic dance music]] festivals commonly use it. Its purported prosocial effects include altered sensations, increased energy, empathy and pleasure, while short-term adverse effects include bruxism, [[Tachycardia|tachycardia]] and sweating. It increases the release of [[Serotonin|serotonin]], [[Dopamine|dopamine]] and norepinephrine in the brain. It is illegal in most jurisdictions but has limited approved medical uses.

British-American rapper, songwriter and record producer. He was raised in Long Beach, [[New York (state)|New York]], and began his career in 1988 with the hip-hop trio KMD. The group disbanded in 1993 after the death of his brother DJ Subroc, and he reemerged in the late 1990s in a metal mask resembling the [[Marvel Comics]] supervillain Doctor Doom. His 2004 album *Madvillainy*, made with the producer Madlib, is often cited as his magnum opus. In 2010, the [[United States]] denied him entry after a tour and forced him back to England. He died in a [[Leeds]] hospital from angioedema after a blood-pressure medication reaction.

British domestic counter-intelligence and security agency, formally the Security Service. Founded in 1909 as the Home Section of the Secret Service Bureau, it arrested enemy spies during [[World War I]]. During [[World War II]] it ran the Double-Cross System, which attempted to turn captured agents to mislead enemy intelligence. After the war it broke up a Soviet spy ring in the early 1970s and was alleged to have monitored [[Trade union|trade unions]] and left-wing politicians. It investigated Irish republican activity in Britain during [[The Troubles]] and later expanded to counter [[Terrorism|terrorism]]. A 1996 law extended its remit to supporting law enforcement against serious crime.

British foreign intelligence agency, formally the Secret Intelligence Service (SIS). It collects human intelligence overseas on foreign nationals in support of its Five Eyes partners. Its chief, known as "C", is directly accountable to the foreign secretary. The name MI6 originated as a wartime label, and its existence was not officially acknowledged until 1994. The Intelligence Services Act 1994 gave it a statutory footing, and it may act only against persons outside the British Islands. Its priorities include counter-terrorism, counter-proliferation and support for cyber security. Some of its actions since the 2000s, including alleged complicity in [[Torture|torture]] and extraordinary rendition, have drawn controversy.

[[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]] program of illegal human experimentation, begun in 1953. It sought drugs and procedures for altering human behavior. Methods included covert high doses of psychoactive drugs, especially [[LSD]], as well as electroshock, hypnosis, sensory deprivation and [[Torture|torture]]. Subjects included unwitting U.S. and Canadian citizens, and research was carried out at more than 80 institutions, including universities, hospitals and prisons. After CIA director Richard Helms ordered the files destroyed in 1973, the program was revealed in 1975 by the Church Committee of the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]]. A 1977 Freedom of Information Act request uncovered 20,000 documents, and some information was declassified in 2001.

Field-effect transistor with an insulated gate, most commonly made by controlled oxidation of [[Silicon|silicon]]. Its gate voltage sets the device's conductivity, letting it amplify or switch signals. The first working MOSFET was invented in 1959 by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at [[Bell Labs]]. Its main advantage is that it needs almost no input current to control the load current at low frequencies. It is by far the most common [[Transistor|transistor]] in digital circuits, with billions included in a memory chip or microprocessor. Complementary pairs of MOS transistors make switching circuits with very low power consumption, as CMOS logic.

Audio coding format using [[Data compression|lossy compression]], developed largely in Germany. Under Karlheinz Brandenburg, the Fraunhofer Society designed it to shrink audio data while still sounding faithful to most listeners. Compared with CD-quality audio, it commonly reduces file size by 75–95%, depending on the [[Bit|bit rate]]. It was defined in 1991 as part of the MPEG-1 standard and extended in MPEG-2. It uses lossy compression to reduce precision and partially discard data. Its small size fueled a boom in music distribution over the [[Internet]] in the late 1990s. The format became associated with copyright infringement and piracy, notably through [[Napster]] and MP3.com.

Transnational criminal [[Gang|gang]] that originated in [[Los Angeles]] in the 1980s. Also known as *Mara Salvatrucha*, it was originally set up to protect Salvadoran immigrants from other gangs. Many members were deported to [[El Salvador]] after the Salvadoran Civil War ended in 1992, helping it spread to [[Central America]]. It has a longtime rivalry with the 18th Street gang. Most members are Central American, particularly Salvadoran. In 2018 its U.S. membership of up to 10,000 accounted for less than 1% of the 1.4 million gang members in the United States. In February 2025 the U.S. government designated MS-13 a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

Operating system for x86-based [[Personal computer|personal computers]], developed mostly by [[Microsoft]]. MS-DOS, an acronym for Microsoft Disk Operating System, was the main operating system for [[IBM]] PC compatibles in the 1980s. IBM released it in 1981 as PC DOS 1.0 for use in its IBM Personal Computer. It began as 86-DOS, written by Tim Paterson and owned by Seattle Computer Products; Microsoft bought it in 1981 and renamed it MS-DOS. Early versions ran on Intel 8086 processors and stored software on [[Floppy disk|floppy disks]]; later releases supported larger storage media and newer processors. MS-DOS went through eight versions before development ceased in 2000; version 6.22 in 1994 was the final standalone release. Versions 7 and 8 mainly loaded [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] 9x, and the command interpreter COMMAND.COM ran whenever no program was running.

Indian cricketer, the only captain to win three different limited-overs ICC tournaments. He captained India in limited-overs formats from 2007 to 2017 and in Test cricket from 2008 to 2014. He led India to victory in the 2007 ICC World Twenty20, the 2011 [[Cricket World Cup]] and the 2013 ICC Champions Trophy. In the [[Indian Premier League]], he captained the [[Chennai]] Super Kings to five titles, in 2010, 2011, 2018, 2021 and 2023. The [[Government of India]] gave him India's highest sporting honour, the Khel Ratna Award, in 2008. He scored 17,266 international runs and was the first wicket-keeper to pass 5,000 IPL runs.
